subtopic_detail: Post-UTI imaging cascade after typical first UTI
stem:
A 14-month-old girl completed a 3 day course of oral trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole for a first febrile urinary tract infection two weeks ago. Urine culture from a clean catch specimen grew Escherichia coli at greater than 10 to the 8 CFU per litre, sensitive to the antibiotic used. Fever settled within 36 hours and she has been well since.

Antenatal ultrasound at 20 weeks was normal and postnatal renal function has never been checked. She had a normal newborn examination and there is no family history of vesicoureteric reflux or renal disease. She is up to date with immunisations, growing along the 50th centile for weight and length, and toilet training is not yet established. There have been no further urinary symptoms.

data_table.Examination: abdomen soft with no palpable masses, external genitalia normal, back and spine unremarkable

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Reassure the family that imaging is not required and give safety-netting advice for future febrile illnesses
options.rationale: RCH does not recommend routine renal tract ultrasound after a single typical E coli UTI in a child aged over 6 months who responded within 48 hours of antibiotics, has normal antenatal imaging, and no atypical features. Safety-netting for early reassessment of any future febrile illness is the appropriate outpatient plan. (Source: RCH CPG: Urinary tract infection)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Urinary tract infection

options.text: Arrange outpatient renal tract ultrasound within 6 weeks with paediatric review of the imaging result
options.rationale: Routine post-UTI ultrasound is a NICE construct, not the RCH pathway. RCH reserves ultrasound for atypical UTI, recurrence, non-E coli organism, sepsis, or infants under 6 months without antenatal imaging - none apply here. (Source: RCH CPG: Urinary tract infection)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Urinary tract infection

options.text: Arrange dimercaptosuccinic acid scanning at 4 to 6 months post-illness to assess for cortical scarring
options.rationale: DMSA is a NICE-recommended follow-up but does not appear in the RCH cascade. The RCH pathway does not use DMSA for a single typical UTI in this age group. (Source: RCH CPG: Urinary tract infection)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Urinary tract infection

options.text: Arrange micturating cystourethrogram to exclude vesicoureteric reflux as an underlying cause
options.rationale: MCUG is invasive, involves urinary catheterisation and ionising radiation, and is not part of the RCH post-UTI cascade for a single typical UTI. It is reserved for selected children with recurrent UTI or abnormal ultrasound findings. (Source: RCH CPG: Urinary tract infection)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Urinary tract infection

options.text: Commence low dose trimethoprim prophylaxis at 2 mg/kg nocte for 12 months with paediatric clinic review
options.rationale: Antibiotic prophylaxis is not recommended after a single typical E coli UTI in a low-risk child. Trials such as PRIVENT show modest benefit only in selected higher-risk populations, and prophylaxis is not first-line here. (Source: RCH CPG: Urinary tract infection)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Urinary tract infection

explanation.summary: This child had an uncomplicated typical E coli UTI that responded promptly to first-line antibiotics. The RCH cascade for imaging after paediatric UTI is more restrictive than NICE and does not require routine imaging in this setting. Safety-netting for early urine testing during any future febrile illness is the correct plan.
key_points: RCH indications for post-UTI ultrasound: age under 6 months without antenatal imaging, atypical UTI, non-E coli organism, poor response at 48 hours, or recurrent UTI
DMSA and MCUG are NICE constructs and are not in the RCH cascade
Antibiotic prophylaxis has a narrow AU indication and is not first-line for a single typical UTI
explanation.pearls: The single strongest driver of over-investigation of paediatric UTI is applying NICE algorithms in Australia. Anchor to RCH and its atypical-UTI trigger list.

stem:
A 5-year-old boy weighing 22 kg attends a general practice for review after his second episode of anaphylaxis to cashew nut, this time triggered by an accidental exposure at kindergarten. On the first exposure two months ago he developed urticaria, lip swelling and audible wheeze that resolved with intramuscular adrenaline administered by paramedics.

Skin prick testing performed by an allergist has confirmed cashew and pistachio sensitisation with wheal sizes above the diagnostic cut-off. He has no other atopic disease, takes no regular medication, and there is no personal or family history of arrhythmia. Both parents have completed ASCIA anaphylaxis first aid training and are able to demonstrate correct injector technique on a trainer device.
lead_in: Which adrenaline autoinjector prescription is most appropriate?

options.text: Two adrenaline 150 microgram autoinjectors with an ASCIA anaphylaxis action plan and instruction to carry both at all times
options.rationale: The 150 microgram device is reserved for children weighing 10 to 20 kg. At 22 kg this child has crossed into the 300 microgram band. (Source: ASCIA Guidelines: Prescribing an adrenaline autoinjector)
source_refs: ASCIA Guidelines: Prescribing an adrenaline autoinjector

options.text: Two adrenaline 300 microgram autoinjectors with an ASCIA anaphylaxis action plan and instruction to carry both at all times
options.rationale: ASCIA prescribes the 300 microgram device for children weighing 20 kg or more using a banded weight rule. Two devices are the standard AU prescription to allow a repeat dose if symptoms do not respond after 5 minutes. (Source: ASCIA Guidelines: Prescribing an adrenaline autoinjector)
source_refs: ASCIA Guidelines: Prescribing an adrenaline autoinjector

options.text: A single adrenaline 300 microgram autoinjector with an ASCIA anaphylaxis action plan and referral to community pharmacy for a second on request
options.rationale: ASCIA advises prescribing two devices simultaneously so a second dose is immediately available at the same location if response is inadequate at 5 minutes. Waiting for a second prescription is unsafe. (Source: ASCIA Guidelines: Prescribing an adrenaline autoinjector)
source_refs: ASCIA Guidelines: Prescribing an adrenaline autoinjector

options.text: A prescription for oral cetirizine 10 mg daily during pollen season with an adrenaline 300 microgram autoinjector as required
options.rationale: Regular antihistamine has no preventive role in food anaphylaxis and does not reduce risk. It also risks masking early urticarial signs of a reaction. (Source: ASCIA Guidelines: Prescribing an adrenaline autoinjector)
source_refs: ASCIA Guidelines: Prescribing an adrenaline autoinjector

options.text: A prescription for daily inhaled fluticasone 100 microgram twice daily and two adrenaline 150 microgram autoinjectors
options.rationale: There is no indication for inhaled corticosteroid without a diagnosis of asthma, and 150 microgram is the wrong band for a 22 kg child. (Source: ASCIA Guidelines: Prescribing an adrenaline autoinjector)
source_refs: ASCIA Guidelines: Prescribing an adrenaline autoinjector

explanation.summary: ASCIA uses a banded weight rule for paediatric adrenaline autoinjectors: 150 microgram for 10 to 20 kg and 300 microgram for 20 kg and above. Two devices should be prescribed together so a repeat dose is available at 5 minutes if needed. This 22 kg boy requires two 300 microgram devices.
key_points: ASCIA banded doses: EpiPen Jr 150 mcg for 10 to 20 kg, EpiPen 300 mcg for 20 kg and above
Prescribe two devices simultaneously; the repeat dose is given after 5 minutes if response is inadequate
Oral antihistamines and daily inhaled corticosteroids have no role in preventing anaphylaxis
explanation.pearls: Do not perform mg/kg arithmetic at the bedside for autoinjectors - use the ASCIA weight bands. The threshold of 20 kg is the one to remember.

sources.label: ASCIA Guidelines: Prescribing an adrenaline autoinjector

subtopic_detail: Gastroenteritis rehydration pathway after failed oral trial
stem:
A 20-month-old girl weighing 12 kg is brought to a regional emergency department with 36 hours of watery diarrhoea and vomiting after a family gastroenteritis outbreak. In the department she has been given a single dose of oral ondansetron 2 mg and offered oral rehydration solution 5 mL every 5 minutes over the past 60 minutes, but has vomited three times and refuses further sips.

On examination she is fractious but consolable. Mucous membranes are dry, capillary refill at the sternum is 3 seconds, and skin turgor is mildly reduced. She has passed a small volume of concentrated urine 4 hours ago. Weight from a well child check 3 weeks ago was 12.5 kg. There is no bilious vomiting, no blood in the stool and no abdominal distension.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse rate 148, blood pressure 92/58, respiratory rate 32, SpO2 99 percent on room air, temperature 37.6 degrees
data_table.Bedside investigations: capillary blood glucose 4.4 mmol/L (3.5-5.5), venous gas pH 7.34 with bicarbonate 20 mmol/L (22-28)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in rehydration?

options.text: Insert an intravenous cannula and commence 0.9 percent sodium chloride at 20 mL/kg over 20 minutes as a resuscitation bolus
options.rationale: A fluid bolus at this rate is reserved for shock, not moderate dehydration. Her perfusion parameters do not meet shock criteria and IV rehydration is second-line to NG in AU paeds practice. (Source: RCH CPG: Gastroenteritis)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Gastroenteritis

options.text: Administer a second oral ondansetron 4 mg dose and continue small-volume oral rehydration solution attempts
options.rationale: The RCH single ondansetron dose for a child of this weight is 2 mg (8 to 15 kg band). A repeat dose is not recommended and 4 mg exceeds the correct band. (Source: RCH CPG: Gastroenteritis)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Gastroenteritis

options.text: Insert a nasogastric tube and commence continuous rehydration with oral rehydration solution at 25 mL/kg/hour for the next 4 hours
options.rationale: In children with mild to moderate dehydration and failure of the oral trial, the RCH pathway is nasogastric rehydration before intravenous fluids. Continuous NG rehydration at approximately 25 mL/kg/hour over 4 hours corrects the deficit. (Source: RCH CPG: Gastroenteritis)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Gastroenteritis

options.text: Admit for observation on maintenance intravenous 0.9 percent sodium chloride with 5 percent dextrose at 44 mL per hour
options.rationale: Maintenance-only IV fluids do not correct the estimated 4 percent deficit efficiently and skip the preferred NG rehydration step. (Source: RCH CPG: Gastroenteritis)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Gastroenteritis

options.text: Discharge home with instructions to continue small volume oral rehydration solution and represent if there is no improvement in 12 hours
options.rationale: Discharge after a failed oral trial with ongoing signs of moderate dehydration is inappropriate. Formal rehydration in the department is required. (Source: RCH CPG: Gastroenteritis)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Gastroenteritis

explanation.summary: This 20-month-old has clinically moderate dehydration and has failed a supervised oral rehydration trial after ondansetron. The RCH pathway then favours nasogastric rehydration before escalating to intravenous therapy, which is reserved for severe dehydration, shock, or NGT failure.
key_points: NG rehydration is first-line after failed oral trial in mild to moderate dehydration
Ondansetron single dose 2 mg for 8 to 15 kg (0.15 mg/kg banded)
IV fluids reserved for shock or failure of NG rehydration
explanation.pearls: The commonest ED anti-pattern is skipping NG rehydration and going straight to IV. The NG route corrects the deficit efficiently and avoids cannulation.

stem:
A 4-year-old boy is brought to a tertiary paediatric emergency department with 24 hours of fever, lethargy, and a non-blanching purpuric rash on the shins and buttocks that appeared this morning. He is now drowsy and difficult to rouse, cool peripherally to the mid-forearm, and has a prolonged capillary refill of 5 seconds at the sternum. He weighs 18 kg.

He is up to date with the National Immunisation Program schedule including meningococcal ACWY and B, and has no known allergies. His mother reports he was well enough to attend day care yesterday morning. He has no significant past medical history and is not on regular medications.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse rate 168, blood pressure 78/40, respiratory rate 44, SpO2 96 percent on room air, temperature 39.8 degrees
data_table.Bedside investigations: capillary blood glucose 5.6 mmol/L (3.5-5.5), venous lactate 4.2 mmol/L (0.5-2.2)

lead_in: After immediate airway assessment and application of monitoring, what is the correct order of the next four interventions?

options.text: Infuse a 20 mL/kg 0.9 percent sodium chloride bolus over 5 minutes, obtain intravenous access afterwards, administer intravenous ceftriaxone 100 mg/kg, then draw blood cultures
options.rationale: A fluid bolus cannot be delivered without access, and cultures should be taken before or with the first antibiotic dose whenever access is available - not after. (Source: RCH CPG: Sepsis - assessment and management)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Sepsis - assessment and management

options.text: Commence a peripheral adrenaline infusion at 0.05 microgram/kg/min, obtain intravenous access, administer intravenous ceftriaxone 100 mg/kg, then draw blood cultures
options.rationale: Inotropes are reserved for fluid-refractory shock after 40 to 60 mL/kg of crystalloid. Starting adrenaline before the first fluid bolus is not the AU sequence. (Source: RCH CPG: Sepsis - assessment and management)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Sepsis - assessment and management

options.text: Draw a lumbar puncture for cerebrospinal fluid, obtain intravenous access, administer intravenous ceftriaxone 100 mg/kg, then infuse a 20 mL/kg 0.9 percent sodium chloride bolus
options.rationale: Lumbar puncture is contraindicated in shock and impaired consciousness. It is deferred until the child is haemodynamically stable and neurologically improved. (Source: RCH CPG: Sepsis - assessment and management)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Sepsis - assessment and management

options.text: Obtain intravenous or intraosseous access, draw blood cultures, administer intravenous ceftriaxone 100 mg/kg, then infuse a 20 mL/kg 0.9 percent sodium chloride bolus over 5 to 10 minutes
options.rationale: The RCH paediatric sepsis pathway sequences access first, then cultures, then first-hour antibiotics, then 20 mL/kg saline bolus over 5 to 10 minutes. Antibiotics must not wait for cultures if cultures cannot be drawn promptly, but with prompt access both can be taken in sequence. (Source: RCH CPG: Sepsis - assessment and management)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Sepsis - assessment and management

options.text: Obtain intravenous access, administer intravenous dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg, draw blood cultures, then infuse a 20 mL/kg 0.9 percent sodium chloride bolus
options.rationale: Dexamethasone is considered adjunctively in pneumococcal meningitis and is given with or before the first antibiotic dose, but it should not replace timely antibiotic delivery in septic shock. (Source: RCH CPG: Sepsis - assessment and management)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Sepsis - assessment and management

explanation.summary: This child has septic shock with purpuric rash suggestive of meningococcaemia. The RCH pathway requires immediate access, cultures, and first-hour antibiotics, followed by 20 mL/kg saline boluses titrated up to 60 mL/kg. Inotropes come only after fluid-refractoriness. LP is deferred while shock persists.
key_points: Order: access, cultures, first antibiotic, 20 mL/kg saline bolus over 5 to 10 minutes
Antibiotics within 1 hour is the AU standard - do not delay for cultures if access is difficult
Adrenaline / noradrenaline reserved for fluid-refractory shock after 40 to 60 mL/kg crystalloid
explanation.pearls: Meningococcal purpura with shock is a national safety pathway. Cef 100 mg/kg IV up to 2 g is the AU empiric dose.

sources.label: RCH CPG: Sepsis - assessment and management

stem:
A term female neonate born at 38 plus 4 weeks by uncomplicated vaginal delivery is reviewed on day 4 of life in the postnatal ward. Her mother is blood group O rhesus positive and the baby is A rhesus positive with a direct antiglobulin test negative and blood groups matched. She is exclusively breastfed with a 6 percent weight loss from birth and is otherwise well.

A transcutaneous bilirubin at 24 hours was 90 micromol/L. On clinical examination today at 96 hours of age she looks jaundiced to the mid-abdomen with normal tone, a strong cry, and no hepatosplenomegaly. Serum total bilirubin drawn is 320 micromol/L, predominantly unconjugated. Full blood count is unremarkable and reticulocyte count is normal.

data_table.Investigations: total bilirubin 320 micromol/L, conjugated bilirubin 8 micromol/L, DAT negative, haemoglobin 175 g/L (150-220), reticulocyte count within normal limits, group and hold A rhesus positive

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Perform an immediate double volume exchange transfusion after commencing intensive triple overhead phototherapy
options.rationale: The exchange transfusion line at 96 hours in a term infant without haemolysis is above 450 micromol/L. Her level is well below this. (Source: NICE CG98 adapted by RCH: Neonatal jaundice)
source_refs: NICE CG98 adapted by RCH: Neonatal jaundice

options.text: Withhold breastfeeding for 48 hours, commence formula supplementation, and repeat the serum bilirubin level in 24 hours
options.rationale: Interrupting breastfeeding is not recommended in AU practice and can compromise establishment. Phototherapy alongside supported breastfeeding is preferred. (Source: NICE CG98 adapted by RCH: Neonatal jaundice)
source_refs: NICE CG98 adapted by RCH: Neonatal jaundice

options.text: Reassure the family that this represents physiological jaundice and arrange community midwife home review in 48 hours
options.rationale: The bilirubin level at 96 hours has crossed the phototherapy threshold and cannot be observed with community review only. (Source: NICE CG98 adapted by RCH: Neonatal jaundice)
source_refs: NICE CG98 adapted by RCH: Neonatal jaundice

options.text: Send urgent haemolysis screen including G6PD, pyruvate kinase and haemoglobin electrophoresis before starting treatment
options.rationale: With DAT negative, blood groups matched, and normal reticulocyte count and haemoglobin, urgent haemolysis screen is not the priority. Phototherapy should not wait for further tests. (Source: NICE CG98 adapted by RCH: Neonatal jaundice)
source_refs: NICE CG98 adapted by RCH: Neonatal jaundice

options.text: Commence single overhead phototherapy, repeat the serum bilirubin in 6 hours, and continue breastfeeding with lactation support
options.rationale: At 96 hours of age a term infant with no haemolysis crosses the AU-adapted NICE phototherapy line at approximately 310 to 320 micromol/L, warranting single phototherapy and a repeat level to check response. Breastfeeding continues alongside. (Source: NICE CG98 adapted by RCH: Neonatal jaundice)
source_refs: NICE CG98 adapted by RCH: Neonatal jaundice

explanation.summary: At 96 hours of age a term neonate with an unconjugated bilirubin of 320 micromol/L and no haemolysis has crossed the phototherapy line on the AU-adapted NICE chart. Treatment is single phototherapy with continued breastfeeding and a 6 hour repeat level. Exchange transfusion is a separate, much higher line reserved for severe or resistant hyperbilirubinaemia.
key_points: Phototherapy threshold at 96 hours in a term infant without haemolysis approximates 310 to 320 micromol/L
Exchange transfusion line is much higher (about 450 micromol/L) and unmet here
Continue breastfeeding with support; do not interrupt for phototherapy alone
explanation.pearls: Read the phototherapy chart by age in hours, not days. The line rises sharply over the first 96 hours and plateaus after that.

sources.label: NICE CG98 adapted by RCH: Neonatal jaundice

stem:
A 22-month-old boy is reviewed in a paediatric assessment unit on day 6 of daily high fevers that have not responded to alternating paracetamol and ibuprofen. His parents describe non-purulent bilateral conjunctival redness that started on day 3, a strawberry appearance to his tongue since yesterday, and a rash on his trunk that has come and gone.

He has no cough, coryza, or diarrhoea. Blood tests today show a C-reactive protein of 90 mg/L (less than 5), erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 60 mm/hour, platelet count of 480 x10 to the 9 per litre, and mild sterile pyuria on urinalysis. Liver enzymes show an alanine aminotransferase of 90 U/L (less than 40). A recent throat swab for group A streptococcus is negative and there are no oral vesicles or exudate. There is no lymphadenopathy over 1.5 cm and no peripheral desquamation yet.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse rate 148, blood pressure 96/58, respiratory rate 32, SpO2 99 percent on room air, temperature 39.4 degrees
data_table.Investigations: CRP 90 mg/L (less than 5), ESR 60 mm/hour, platelets 480 x10 to the 9 per litre (150-400), ALT 90 U/L (less than 40), albumin 30 g/L (35-50), urinalysis with sterile pyuria

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Arrange an urgent echocardiogram and commence intravenous immunoglobulin 2 g/kg with aspirin 3 to 5 mg/kg daily
options.rationale: Fever for 5 or more days with 2 to 3 clinical criteria plus supportive laboratory features (CRP over 30, ESR over 40, thrombocytosis, sterile pyuria, elevated ALT, low albumin) meets the AHA incomplete Kawasaki disease pathway. Treatment with IVIG plus aspirin should not wait for the echocardiogram. (Source: RCH CPG: Kawasaki Disease)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Kawasaki Disease

options.text: Continue supportive care with paracetamol and reassess in 48 hours before considering any specific therapy
options.rationale: Delaying IVIG beyond day 10 doubles the risk of coronary aneurysm. Fever on day 6 with matching criteria warrants treatment now. (Source: RCH CPG: Kawasaki Disease)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Kawasaki Disease

options.text: Commence intravenous benzylpenicillin for suspected scarlet fever and repeat throat swab in 48 hours
options.rationale: Group A streptococcal throat swab is negative and there are no oral or pharyngeal features to support scarlet fever. Antibiotic therapy will not address the underlying vasculitis. (Source: RCH CPG: Kawasaki Disease)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Kawasaki Disease

options.text: Commence oral prednisolone 2 mg/kg daily as first-line monotherapy pending confirmation of coronary artery involvement
options.rationale: Steroids are used as adjuncts to IVIG in high-risk or IVIG-refractory disease, not as first-line monotherapy in AU practice. (Source: RCH CPG: Kawasaki Disease)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Kawasaki Disease

options.text: Arrange a lumbar puncture and commence intravenous ceftriaxone 100 mg/kg for suspected meningitis
options.rationale: There are no meningitic features and the presentation over 6 days with mucocutaneous features points to Kawasaki disease, not meningitis. (Source: RCH CPG: Kawasaki Disease)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Kawasaki Disease

explanation.summary: Prolonged fever with fewer than 4 principal Kawasaki criteria but supportive laboratory features fulfils the incomplete Kawasaki disease pathway. IVIG plus aspirin should be started promptly. Delay beyond day 10 markedly increases the risk of coronary artery aneurysm.
key_points: Incomplete KD: 5 or more days of fever, 2 to 3 principal criteria, plus supportive labs (CRP over 30, ESR over 40, thrombocytosis, sterile pyuria, raised ALT, low albumin)
IVIG 2 g/kg single dose plus aspirin 3 to 5 mg/kg daily
Do not delay treatment for echocardiogram - the two can proceed in parallel
explanation.pearls: The single strongest predictor of long-term coronary sequelae is IVIG delay past day 10. Recognise the incomplete pattern early.

sources.label: AHA Scientific Statement: Diagnosis, Treatment and Long-Term Management of Kawasaki Disease
